record.name: Agentic AI in Federal Contracting
record.description: The article examines the adoption of agentic AI across US federal contracting offices, noting that 53% of agencies are exploring or planning agentic pilots and 15% already use such systems. It warns that these agents autonomously plan and act across multiple systems without waiting for human approval, upending traditional accountability structures built around person-executed steps. The author argues that agencies must establish data governance, identity systems, and rigorous traceability before scaling autonomy.
record.novelty: The piece proposes treating autonomy as a “dial, not a switch” by starting with narrowly scoped allowable actions and forcing escalation to humans when confidence thresholds are not met. It also emphasizes that in classified, air-gapped environments, the harder problem is not orchestration but proving trustworthiness through FedRAMP-level logging, chain-of-custody governance, and attributable audit trails for every agent action.
record.stakeholders: Federal contracting offices, government contractors, oversight and audit bodies, and AI vendors such as Blackstraw AI are involved in developing, deploying, and governing these systems.
record.agentic_rationale: The source states that agentic AI “plans and acts across multiple systems without pausing for permission,” and can autonomously “draft acquisition packages or routes workflow tasks” and “execute a process across systems.” These systems handle routine cases end-to-end, escalating only when confidence thresholds are not met, leaving a full trail of prompts and handoffs.
record.tech_details: The article notes that agentic models must operate in classified, air-gapped environments that do not naturally support cross-system reach, requiring carefully rethought architecture to prevent unsafe segmentation bridging. It highlights the need for robust identity systems, access governance, and traceability infrastructure that logs every prompt, query, and document route to satisfy strict scrutiny standards.

record.name: ADVOCATE program
record.organisation: Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H)
record.description: ARPA-H launched the four-year, $62.7 million ADVOCATE program to develop patient-facing agentic AI, a supervisory AI layer, and scalable deployment strategies for heart failure care across the United States. The initiative aims to deliver 24/7 cardiac care to all Americans—including those in rural counties without cardiologists—by creating autonomous clinical agents that monitor patients and support treatment between doctor visits. Contract awards have been issued to teams including Kaiser Permanente, Duke University, Stanford University, Atman Health, Updoc, and Tempus AI, with up to $33.7 million committed in the first year.
record.novelty: It seeks to create the first FDA-authorized patient-facing autonomous clinical AI that acts as a "clinician-extender" capable of providing certain care autonomously between visits. It also introduces a disease-agnostic supervisory AI layer to continuously monitor clinical agents for unsafe recommendations and out-of-distribution behavior in real time, developed alongside a new FDA regulatory framework.
record.stakeholders: Heart failure patients (especially in rural and underserved communities), Medicare and the broader U.S. healthcare system, clinical care teams, ARPA-H, the FDA, and the contracted development and deployment teams (Kaiser Permanente, Duke, Stanford, Atman Health, Updoc, Tempus AI) and participating health systems using Epic and Cerner EHRs.
record.agentic_rationale: The patient-facing AI is designed to "act as an autonomous member of the clinical team" that is "capable of providing certain care autonomously" between regular doctor visits, "adjusts on the fly to ask each patient relevant diagnostic questions," and escalates issues to human clinicians when needed. A separate supervisory AI will continuously monitor these clinical agents by "detecting unsafe recommendations and out-of-distribution behavior in real time."
record.tech_details: Patient-facing systems use large language models with voice interfaces (Atman Health), extend the Olivia patient health app with continuous deep clinical monitoring (Tempus AI), and apply clinician-built rules for conversational validation of proposed actions (Updoc). The supervisory AI uses a three-stage pipeline with outlier filtering, rule-based screening and a deep-research auditing agent (Stanford), while deployment will integrate into Epic and Cerner/Oracle electronic health records across 21 medical centers and rural sites.

record.name: AWS Wickr tactical communications with agentic AI

record.name: OMB M-25-21 Federal AI Compliance Deadline
record.organisation: Office of Management and Budget; Department of Homeland Security
record.description: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 established a September 22, 2026 compliance deadline requiring federal agencies to implement minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI or discontinue those systems. The Department of Homeland Security is exploiting a “principal basis” loophole to avoid classifying consequential autonomous systems—including Anduril’s Autonomous Surveillance Tower and Palantir’s ELICE—as high-impact, thereby circumventing mandatory safeguards like pre-deployment testing and human oversight.
record.novelty: The compliance deadline was designed to force a comprehensive federal inventory and accountability for high-impact AI, but the memo’s White House page now returns a 404 error and DHS is narrowly interpreting “principal basis” to shield systems that independently flag targets and dictate enforcement deployments from oversight.
record.stakeholders: Federal agencies, DHS and ICE officers, individuals subject to border surveillance and deportation targeting, and the general public affected by AI-driven enforcement decisions.
record.agentic_rationale: The Autonomous Surveillance Tower “independently selects what to ignore and what to flag,” and its alerts “dictate where agents are dispatched,” with border officials “entirely dependent on its output.” Palantir’s ELICE “identify and prioritize addresses for enforcement, leading agents to locations they would not otherwise know to target.”
record.tech_details: Anduril’s Autonomous Surveillance Tower uses AI to detect persons, vehicles, or animals and autonomously determine what to flag or ignore. record.name: Sovereign Government Operating System

The architecture uses APIs, GraphQL, and open-source components to enable cross-agency interoperability, data custodianship, and consent management. It also outlines a “Sovereign AI” layer where agents receive scoped identities and delegated authority to perform transactions on behalf of citizens.
record.novelty: It treats AI agent governance as a core infrastructure problem rather than an application feature, assigning software agents their own digital identities, scoped delegation, and audit trails within the government access-control architecture. The model explicitly requires traceable AI-assisted decisions and policy-governed API access before agents can operate across sensitive government datasets.
record.stakeholders: African government agencies seeking cross-agency interoperability, citizens who would use wallet-based digital identities and agent-assisted services, and technology vendors providing sovereign cloud and open-source infrastructure.
record.agentic_rationale: The framework envisions software agents that "can make requests without a person manually initiating every interaction" and perform government transactions on behalf of a taxpayer, requiring the system to establish which agent acted, what authority it had and who delegated that authority. Agents operate within delegated authority while keeping officers involved in high-impact decisions, creating a boundary around autonomous action.
record.tech_details: The architecture is API- and GraphQL-based, incorporating a metadata registry, access-control and data-orchestration layer, API gateway, consent and authorisation registry, unified IAM, and audit logging, with sovereign cloud and sovereign AI underneath; it references open-source ecosystems such as X-Road, GovStack, and OpenNDX.
